To xeriscape means to design, plant, or convert a garden or landscape so that it needs very little water to survive — ideally thriving mostly on natural rainfall alone.

Imagine you have a garden. A normal garden might be full of lush green grass and plants that need to be watered every day, especially in summer. That uses a huge amount of water.

When you xeriscape that garden, you replace it — or redesign it — so that the plants, soil, and layout work together to get by with as little water as possible. You might be doing this because you live in a dry climate, because water is expensive, or simply because you want to be environmentally responsible.

So: to xeriscape something is to make it survive and look good with minimal water.
What actually happens when someone xeriscapes:

When you xeriscape a garden or yard, you typically do a combination of these things:

  • Replace thirsty plants with drought-tolerant ones. Ordinary lawns and ornamental flowers often need frequent watering. When you xeriscape, you swap these out for plants that are naturally adapted to dry conditions — things like native wildflowers, ornamental grasses, lavender, rosemary, succulents, or cacti. These plants have evolved to store water or survive with very little of it.
  • Get rid of, or drastically reduce, the lawn. Grass lawns are among the thirstiest things you can grow. Xeriscaping often involves replacing grassy areas with gravel, mulch, stone pathways, ground-hugging plants, or decorative rock beds.
  • Improve the soil. Healthy soil holds moisture better, so plants don't need to be watered as frequently. Xeriscaping may involve adding compost or other organic matter to the soil to help it retain whatever water it does receive.
  • Use mulch generously. A thick layer of mulch (shredded bark, wood chips, etc.) spread around plants slows evaporation from the soil. This keeps moisture in the ground longer, so plants stay hydrated even without frequent watering.
  • Install efficient irrigation if needed. Rather than overhead sprinklers that waste water through evaporation, xeriscaping uses drip irrigation — a system that delivers water slowly and directly to the base of each plant, right where the roots can absorb it.
  • Group plants by water need. If some plants need slightly more water than others, they're placed together in one zone. Plants that need very little water are grouped in another zone. This way, you're not over-watering drought-tolerant plants just because they're planted next to something thirstier.
  • Plan the layout smartly. Shade from trees or walls reduces evaporation. Slopes and contours of the land are designed to direct rainwater toward plants rather than letting it run off into the street.
A key nuance — it's not just about cacti and rocks:

Many people assume that when you xeriscape, you end up with a bare, dusty yard full of rocks and spiky cacti. That's one approach, and it works in desert climates — but it's not the only outcome. A well-xeriscaped garden can be lush, colorful, and beautiful. It simply achieves that beauty using plants and methods that are matched to the local climate, so that nature does most of the work of keeping them alive.

The goal isn't bareness — it's efficiency. You're not trying to make a garden look like the moon. You're trying to make a garden that is self-sustaining and water-smart.

• People in hot, dry regions (like the American Southwest, parts of Australia, or the Mediterranean) xeriscape because water is genuinely scarce or expensive there.
  • Homeowners xeriscape to lower their water bills significantly — a xeriscaped yard can use 50–75% less water than a conventional garden.
  • Cities and municipalities sometimes xeriscape public parks and roadsides to reduce water use at a large scale.
  • People who care about conservation xeriscape because it reduces strain on local water supplies, helps local wildlife by using native plants, and requires fewer chemical fertilizers and pesticides.
How the verb is used in sentences:

• "After the drought, they decided to xeriscape their entire front yard." (They converted it.)
  • "She is xeriscaping the community garden to cut costs." (She is in the process of converting it.)
  • "The city has xeriscaped all its highway medians." (The city completed the conversion.)
  • "If you live in a dry climate, you should consider xeriscaping." (Using the method.)

To xeriscape is to thoughtfully redesign a landscape — choosing the right plants, soil, and water systems — so that it can thrive beautifully on very little water. It's both an act and an ongoing approach: a way of thinking about land that puts water conservation at the center of every decision, without sacrificing the beauty or life of the garden.
